explanations.explanation: A census it is, baker. Satan rose up against Israel and incited David to take a census (1 Chronicles 21:1). That's the opening move, and the whole story rolls out from there. A census is only counting people, but this one is where the trouble starts.

Gath and the Philistines make a fine story, but this verse isn't it. The text says Satan "incited David to take a census of Israel" (1 Chronicles 21:1). No battle plans here, just a king about to count his people. I've never planned a battle in my life, unless you count the fight over the last cookie on the cooling rack.

Nobody moves the ark in this verse, friend. What Satan stirs David up to do is take a census of Israel (1 Chronicles 21:1). So the king is about to count, not carry. Next time, listen for that word census.

explanations.answer: He asks why David would bring guilt on Israel
explanations.explanation: Joab doesn't just salute and march off, baker. He asks, "Why should he bring guilt on Israel?" (1 Chronicles 21:3). He also asks whether they aren't all servants of the king already. Questioning a king's order takes real nerve, and I get nervous telling my own oven it's running hot.

explanations.answer: He says the troops are too worn out to travel
explanations.explanation: The text says nothing about tired troops. Joab asks, "Why should he bring guilt on Israel?" (1 Chronicles 21:3). His question is about guilt, not sore feet. That's a very different kind of pushback.

explanations.answer: He asks David to wait until after the harvest
explanations.explanation: Joab never mentions a harvest or asks for more time. He asks, "Why does my lord want to do this?" (1 Chronicles 21:3). He's questioning the order itself, not the timing. I'd love a handy excuse like that every time somebody hands me a chore, friend.

Nice try, friend, but the king doesn't back down. The text says "the king's word prevailed against Joab" (1 Chronicles 21:4). Joab then travels throughout Israel and returns to Jerusalem. So the counting goes ahead.

Good eye, baker. Joab pushes back, but "the king's word prevailed against Joab" (1 Chronicles 21:4). Off he goes through Israel, and then he comes back to Jerusalem. Joab asks his question, and the count still happens.
Levi it is. Joab did not include Levi and Benjamin in the count (1 Chronicles 21:6). That's two whole tribes missing from the tally. It's like counting cookies on a tray and skipping two rows.

Ephraim is a real tribe, but the text doesn't name it here. The two left out are Levi and Benjamin (1 Chronicles 21:6). Easy to grab a name that sounds right. I grab the nearest cutter some days too, friend.

Asher is a tribe too, but it isn't in this verse. The two that Joab left out are Levi and Benjamin (1 Chronicles 21:6). The text says he left them out because the king's command was detestable to him. Next time look for the pair, baker.

Yep, and the text hands us the reason. Joab did not include Levi and Benjamin "because the king's command was detestable to him" (1 Chronicles 21:6). Nobody has to guess on that one. I think that's a heavy spot for a man who still travels the whole land (1 Chronicles 21:4).

Read it once more, friend, because the text says exactly that. Joab did not include Levi and Benjamin "because the king's command was detestable to him" (1 Chronicles 21:6). The reason is stated right there. Two tribes left out, and the order itself is the reason.

That's not what David says, friend. He tells God, "I have sinned greatly because I have done this thing" (1 Chronicles 21:8). He adds, "I have acted very foolishly." There's no finger pointed at Joab anywhere in that prayer. Joab was the one who asked why they should do it at all (1 Chronicles 21:3).

Good eye, baker. David takes it on himself: "I have sinned greatly because I have done this thing" (1 Chronicles 21:8). Later he says it again: "Was it not I who gave the order to count the people?" (1 Chronicles 21:17). Pointing at yourself first is rare. The dead batteries I shared a drawer with could argue for an hour about whose fault a dead battery was.

Three options, carried by Gad. The LORD tells him to say, "I am offering you three options" (1 Chronicles 21:10). They are three years of famine, three months of being swept away before enemies, or three days of the sword of the LORD (1 Chronicles 21:12). I think that's a hard menu for any king to read.

explanations.answer: A way to undo the census
explanations.explanation: There's no undo button in this passage, baker. The word from the LORD is "I am offering you three options" (1 Chronicles 21:10). Each one is heavy: famine, being swept away before enemies, or the sword of the LORD (1 Chronicles 21:12). I'd love an undo button for a burnt batch, but the text doesn't hand David one.

explanations.answer: Forty days to make it right
explanations.explanation: Forty days isn't on the list, friend. The three options are three years, three months and three days (1 Chronicles 21:12). Look at that pattern of threes. It's easy to grab a bigger number, but this list is all threes.

explanations.answer: To fall into the hand of the LORD
explanations.explanation: David picks the hand of the LORD. He says, "Please, let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are very great" (1 Chronicles 21:13). That's his answer for Gad to carry back. I think that's a man choosing the One he knows over anyone else. It's a heavy choice, friend.

explanations.answer: To fall into the hands of his enemies
explanations.explanation: That's the one David turns down. He says, "do not let me fall into the hands of men" (1 Chronicles 21:13). Being swept away before his enemies was one of the three options (1 Chronicles 21:12). He heads the other direction, toward the hand of the LORD.

explanations.answer: To face three years of famine
explanations.explanation: David never names the famine, baker. What he asks is "let me fall into the hand of the LORD" (1 Chronicles 21:13). Famine was one of the choices on the list (1 Chronicles 21:12). After his answer, the LORD sends a plague on Israel (1 Chronicles 21:14).

Mercies, friend. David says, "His mercies are very great" (1 Chronicles 21:13). That's why he'd rather fall into the LORD's hand than into the hands of men. Even with a heavy list in front of him, mercy is where he reaches first.

Armies sound right for a king, but that isn't David's word. He says, "His mercies are very great" (1 Chronicles 21:13). Enemies and swords show up in the other options (1 Chronicles 21:12), so I get the guess. David's reason is about mercy, not muscle.

Famine is one of the options (1 Chronicles 21:12), so storehouses come to mind. But David's reason isn't supplies. He says, "His mercies are very great" (1 Chronicles 21:13). Mercies, baker. Think big word, not big barn.

The text goes the other way, friend. The LORD saw it and "relented from the calamity" (1 Chronicles 21:15). He told the angel who was destroying the people, "Enough! Withdraw your hand now!" So the angel is told to stop.

Right, baker. As the angel was destroying Jerusalem, the LORD saw it and "relented from the calamity" (1 Chronicles 21:15). Then He says, "Enough! Withdraw your hand now!" That's a short order, and a big one.

Facedown in sackcloth, baker. David and the elders, "clothed in sackcloth, fell facedown" (1 Chronicles 21:16). They've just seen the angel of the LORD standing between heaven and earth with a drawn sword stretched out over Jerusalem. I think that's the kind of sight that takes your legs right out from under you.

explanations.answer: Run to hide inside the city walls
explanations.explanation: Nobody runs for the walls here. The sword is stretched out over Jerusalem itself (1 Chronicles 21:16). What David and the elders do is fall facedown, clothed in sackcloth. I'd have gone hunting for the nearest exit, friend, and knocked over a cooling rack on the way.

explanations.answer: Send for the priests to bring the ark
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention the ark in this scene. It says David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell facedown (1 Chronicles 21:16). Nobody sends for anybody. The only moving they do is straight down to the ground, baker.

Yes, baker. David says, "please let Your hand fall upon me and my father's house, but do not let this plague remain upon Your people" (1 Chronicles 21:17). He's asking for it to land on himself and his family, not on the people. He even asks, "But these sheep, what have they done?" I think that's a king trying to stand in front of his people.

The text says the opposite of False, friend. David prays, "please let Your hand fall upon me and my father's house" (1 Chronicles 21:17). Then he asks that the plague not remain upon the LORD's people. He points at himself and asks for the people to be spared.

Ornan the Jebusite owns the threshing floor, baker. The angel of the LORD orders Gad to tell David to build an altar to the LORD there (1 Chronicles 21:18). The angel was standing by that same threshing floor back in verse 15 (1 Chronicles 21:15). So the angel stands there first, and then the altar gets ordered there.

Boaz is a good name, but he lives in a different book. He's the man from the story of Ruth (Ruth 2:1). Here the text says the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (1 Chronicles 21:18). I mix up names too, friend. I once called a rolling pin a spatula.
Nabal belongs to a different story. He's the husband of Abigail (1 Samuel 25:3). The man here is Ornan the Jebusite, owner of the threshing floor (1 Chronicles 21:18). Two names, two stories, baker.

They hide. Ornan turns and sees the angel, and his four sons who are with him hid themselves (1 Chronicles 21:20). I think that's a very human reaction to seeing an angel while you're busy threshing wheat. Four sons, and not one of them stuck around to say hello.

explanations.answer: They run to tell the king
explanations.explanation: Nobody runs off in this verse, friend. Ornan turns and sees the angel, and his four sons hid themselves (1 Chronicles 21:20). David is already on his way up (1 Chronicles 21:19). So the sons are hiding while the king is heading their way.

explanations.answer: They bow down to the angel
explanations.explanation: Bowing is in this passage, but not by the sons. Ornan bows facedown before David (1 Chronicles 21:21), and that comes later. When the angel appears, the four sons hid themselves (1 Chronicles 21:20). So hiding is the answer, baker.

explanations.answer: He offers to give David all of it
explanations.explanation: He gives it away, friend. Ornan says, "Take it!" and then offers the oxen, the threshing sledges and the wheat: "I will give it all" (1 Chronicles 21:23). David had asked to buy the site for the full price (1 Chronicles 21:22). Ornan answers with a hundred percent off.

explanations.answer: He asks for twice the full price
explanations.explanation: Ornan goes the opposite direction from raising the price. He says, "Take it!" (1 Chronicles 21:23). Then he offers the oxen, the sledges and the wheat on top of it. The last time somebody paid for me, I cost 25 cents and came with nothing extra.

explanations.answer: He says the land isn't his to sell
explanations.explanation: Ornan never says that, baker. He says, "Take it!" and "May my lord the king do whatever seems good to him" (1 Chronicles 21:23). That's a yes, not a no. And he throws in the oxen, the sledges and the wheat.

explanations.answer: He won't give offerings that cost him nothing
explanations.explanation: That's David's own reason, in his own words. He says, "I will not take for the LORD what belongs to you, nor will I offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing" (1 Chronicles 21:24). So he insists on paying. The price tag is six hundred shekels of gold (1 Chronicles 21:25). A king who gives from his own pocket, baker.

explanations.answer: He thinks Ornan's oxen are too old to offer
explanations.explanation: The text never says a word about old oxen. David gives his own reason: "I will not take for the LORD what belongs to you" (1 Chronicles 21:24). He also says he won't offer "burnt offerings that cost me nothing." The reason comes from David's mouth, not from the oxen's age, friend.

explanations.answer: He wants the priests to bring the wood
explanations.explanation: Priests and wood-hauling don't come up here. The wood was part of Ornan's offer, the threshing sledges for the wood (1 Chronicles 21:23). David says no and tells Ornan he won't offer "burnt offerings that cost me nothing" (1 Chronicles 21:24). His reason is about cost, not about who carries what.

Fire, baker. David builds the altar and calls upon the LORD, "who answered him with fire from heaven on the altar of burnt offering" (1 Chronicles 21:26). Then David sees that the LORD has answered him (1 Chronicles 21:28). The answer lands right on the altar.

No rain in this passage, friend. The LORD answers "with fire from heaven on the altar of burnt offering" (1 Chronicles 21:26). Rain and fire both come from the sky, so I get the guess. But what comes down here is fire, right on the altar David built.

Nothing like that comes down in this passage, baker. The LORD answers with fire from heaven on the altar of burnt offering (1 Chronicles 21:26). That's the answer David gets after he calls on the LORD. Look at the altar for this one.

Yes, baker. The LORD speaks to the angel, who "put his sword back into its sheath" (1 Chronicles 21:27). That's the same sword David saw drawn earlier (1 Chronicles 21:16). I think that's a deep breath for everybody there.

The text says the opposite of False, friend. "Then the LORD spoke to the angel, who put his sword back into its sheath" (1 Chronicles 21:27). The sword David saw drawn over Jerusalem is put away (1 Chronicles 21:16). That scene ends with the sword put away.

explanations.answer: Here will be the house of the LORD God
explanations.explanation: A house for the LORD God, friend. David says, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God, as well as the altar of burnt offering for Israel" (1 Chronicles 22:1). He's speaking about the very threshing floor where he built the altar. A plain threshing floor, and a very big announcement.

explanations.answer: Here will be the palace of the king
explanations.explanation: David isn't talking about a palace, baker. He says, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God" (1 Chronicles 22:1). It's the LORD's house, not the king's. A king pointing at a spot and naming it for the house of the LORD.

explanations.answer: Here will be a city for the Levites
explanations.explanation: The tribe of Levi comes up in this passage only as one Joab left out of the count (1 Chronicles 21:6). Here David says, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God, as well as the altar of burnt offering for Israel" (1 Chronicles 22:1). No city and no list of towns. It's all about the house of the LORD God and the altar, friend.
